trend_write.why: The review step changes how agent work gets checked.
trend_write.post:
people building with coding agents
the new review mode changes how you ship.

Claude Code 3 is trending this morning, and most of the posts are about one feature: the agent now reviews its own diff before it asks you to accept it.

That sounds small. It is not, because the slowest part of agent work was never the writing. It was you reading 400 lines of changes to find the one that breaks the build.

What the review step does, according to the release notes:

1. It runs your test command after every edit.
2. It reads the diff again and lists the risky lines first.
3. It stops and asks when a change touches files outside the task.

The third point matters most. Agents drift. You ask for a fix in one component and get a refactor of three. A hard stop on scope keeps the diff small enough to read.

What to do with it today:

- Put your real test command in the project instructions, or the review has nothing to run.
- Keep tasks narrow. One bug, one change, one review.
- Read the risky lines it lists before anything else.

The cost: every review round takes time and tokens. On a tiny change it is slower than reading the diff yourself.

So turn it on for anything that touches more than one file, and leave it off for one-line fixes.

article_write.title: Two overnight Claude Code builds cost $287. The cheaper one won.
article_write.body:
Two overnight builds cost $287.82. The cheaper one scored higher.

That surprised me, so I went through both runs line by line to see where the money went.

## The setup

Every night Claude Code builds one project alone, capped at 7 hours and $160 per session. An Opus critic scores screenshots, and anything under 8 out of 10 goes back for fixes.

- Build one: a chess engine, $113.65, 3.7 hours, 270 turns.
- Build two: a heart simulation, $174.17, 4.5 hours, 387 turns.

## Where the money went

**Most of the extra cost came from fix rounds, not from the first draft.** The heart build spent its second hour chasing a rendering bug the critic kept flagging.

The chess build had a clear spec. The heart build had a vague one, and vague specs make the agent explore.

## What I changed

1. Every brief now names the three numbers the screen must show.
2. The critic gets the brief too, so it stops asking for things nobody wanted.
3. A build that fails the same check twice stops early.

## Recap

- Clear specs are cheaper than smart models.
- Fix rounds are where budgets die.
- Stop loops that repeat the same failure.

I post a Claude Code thread every morning and a new Claude Studio build every night. Follow along if you want the next bill.

teaser_write.post:
people running claude code overnight
one number predicted my whole bill.

Two nights ago Claude Code built a project on my PC while I slept. In the morning the cost was higher than the cap I had set for it.

Nothing had gone wrong. The cap did exactly what I told it to do. That was the part that bothered me.

So I went through both overnight builds line by line. Every session, every fix round, every turn.

One of them cost 53% more than the other. It was not the harder model or the longer prompt that explained it.

The answer was sitting in a number I had never looked at. Once I saw it, I could predict what the next build would cost before it started.

I also found the gate in my tool pipeline that throws away more good tools than any other. I built it myself and never noticed.

If you let an agent work while nobody watches, you are making the same bet I was.

I wrote down everything I found, with the real numbers, in the article below.
